ACTIONS SECRET LEAK CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your GitHub Actions workflow leak a secret its own masking can't catch?

GitHub Actions masks the exact, unmodified string of a declared secret everywhere it appears in a log. It does not survive two common things: transforming a secret (base64, hex, a substring) before printing produces a different string the masking doesn't recognise, and exporting a secret-derived value to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT doesn't register it for masking at all — a later step that echoes it prints it in plain text. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds both, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --format sarif   # SARIF 2.1.0, for github/codeql-action/upload-sarif
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Common questions

Doesn't GitHub Actions already mask secrets in logs?

Yes, for the exact, unmodified string of a declared secrets.* value (or an env: var sourced from one) — the runner replaces every verbatim occurrence of that string in log output, including inside set -x trace output. This tool does not flag that case. It flags the two documented ways a value still reaches a log unmasked: transforming the secret first, and exporting a secret-derived value without registering it for masking.

Why does transforming a secret bypass masking?

GitHub's masking is an exact string match against the known secret value. base64, hex, case-folding, a substring, or any other re-encoding produces a different string than the one the runner is watching for, so the transformed output prints in plain text even though the original secret would have been masked.

Why is writing a secret to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT a separate risk?

Writing a value there exports it to later steps, but does not register it with the runner's masking list on its own. Only the exact string of a value GitHub already knows is a declared secret gets auto-masked. A freshly derived value — an OAuth token minted using a secret, a signed URL, a session cookie — is not on that list at all, so the first later step that echoes it prints it in plain text unless the workflow calls ::add-mask:: on it first.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my secrets are safe?

No. This checks two specific, well-documented patterns within a single step's YAML text. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your secrets' overall safety. A transform split across two steps, a custom action that re-exports a secret internally, or a transform utility this tool does not recognise are all outside what a regex/indentation scan can see.

More: why GitHub Actions secret masking fails on a transformed value, and this checker vs. reading the workflow by eye.

vs-reading-the-workflow-by-eye.html.text:
← Actions Secret Leak Check

This checker vs. reading the workflow by eye

Reviewing a workflow diff is the normal way a leaked secret gets caught, and it works well for the obvious case -- a step that echoes secrets.TOKEN straight into the log. GitHub's own masking already closes that one anyway. Both of the gaps this checker exists for are quieter than that, and neither looks wrong on a quick read.

What reading the diff catches

A reviewer scanning a pull request for a secrets problem is pattern-matching for the shape everyone already knows to look for: a run: line that prints a secrets.* reference directly, or passes it somewhere it obviously should not go. That pattern-match is fast, and it is right often enough that it is the standard first line of defence. It is also, by construction, blind to anything that does not match the pattern.

What this checker looks for instead

Paste your workflow YAML, or run check.py against a checkout, and it scans every step's text for two specific, well-documented patterns that do not resemble a leak on a visual scan: a value derived from a secret by base64/hex/substring before it is printed, and a value written to $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT/$GITHUB_STATE without a matching ::add-mask::. Same rule, applied to every line, every time -- not a replacement for review, a check for the two things review is least likely to catch under time pressure.

Reading the diff by eyeThis checker
Catches echo ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} immediately -- and GitHub's own masking already catches it too, so the review effort is spent on a case that was already covered. Does not re-flag what GitHub already masks; it looks specifically for the two documented ways a secret-derived value still reaches a log unmasked.
A base64/hex/substring transform reads as ordinary string manipulation three lines from the secrets: reference, with nothing to flag it as the same secret in disguise. Recognises the transform functions GitHub itself documents as masking-defeating and flags the derived value regardless of how far it sits from the original reference.
A write to $GITHUB_OUTPUT looks like completely normal step-to-step data passing -- nothing marks a freshly derived token as something that needed its own ::add-mask:: call. Flags an export of a secret-derived value that was never registered for masking, whether or not anything downstream ever echoes it.
Depends on the reviewer already knowing both gaps exist and checking for them on every line of every workflow, every time. Applies the same two checks consistently, and can be wired into CI with --fail-on-risk so a new finding blocks the merge before a reviewer sees it.

Common questions

Why doesn't code review catch a transformed secret?

A reviewer scanning a diff is pattern-matching for the obvious shape -- echo ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} -- which GitHub's own masking already catches anyway. A base64, hex, case-fold, or substring transform three lines away from the secrets: reference does not look like a leak on a quick read; it looks like ordinary string manipulation. Recognising that the transformed output still fully reverses back to the secret requires tracing the value through the transform, which is exactly the kind of mechanical check a reviewer skimming a PR under time pressure is least likely to do.

Why doesn't code review catch an unmasked $GITHUB_OUTPUT export?

Writing a value to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT looks completely ordinary in a diff -- it is how a step is supposed to pass data to the next one. Nothing about the line itself signals that the value being exported was freshly derived from a secret (an OAuth token minted from it, a signed URL, a session cookie) and was therefore never registered on GitHub's masking list. A reviewer would have to know the specific rule (derived values need their own ::add-mask:: call) and trace the value back to its secret source across steps to catch it, which a visual scan does not do.

Is a human reviewer worse at this than a tool, generally?

No -- a reviewer catches things a regex scan cannot: whether the transform is even necessary, whether the workflow should be using OIDC instead of a long-lived secret at all, whether the whole step belongs in CI. What this checker adds is narrow and mechanical: two specific, well-documented masking gaps, checked the same way on every line, which is exactly the kind of check that is easy to skip when reading quickly and easy to run automatically.

Does this replace code review?

No. It is a static, step-scoped line scanner over workflow YAML text, not a security audit and not a substitute for a reviewer's judgment about whether a secret should be in the workflow at all. Wiring --fail-on-risk into CI catches the two specific patterns it knows before merge; a reviewer is still the one deciding everything else.

Nothing here says code review is a bad way to catch a secrets problem -- it is the right first line of defence for the case it is good at. This page describes the two specific, narrow cases that a visual scan is structurally unlikely to catch, not a fault in reviewers.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML, or run check.py against a checkout, and see whether either pattern is present -- the two checks a diff review is least likely to run.

why-github-actions-secret-masking-fails..text:
← Actions Secret Leak Check

Why GitHub Actions secret masking fails on a transformed value

GitHub Actions masking works by watching a job's log output stream for the exact, literal string of every declared secret (and any env: var sourced from one), and replacing it with *** before the log is stored. That is a string match, not a data-flow analysis — it has no notion of "derived from a secret", only "is this secret's exact value present right here".

Transform the secret before it reaches the log, and the string the runner is watching for is no longer the string it sees:

- env:
    API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
  run: |
    echo "fingerprint: $(echo -n "$API_TOKEN" | base64)"

The base64 encoding of API_TOKEN is a different byte string than API_TOKEN itself. GitHub is watching for the original; it never sees it, so nothing gets masked, and the encoded secret — which still fully reverses back to the original with one command — sits in the log in plain text. Hex encoding, case-folding, a substring (${API_TOKEN:0:8}), URL-encoding, or piping through tr/rev/iconv all have the identical effect: same underlying secret, different string, masking doesn't fire.

The second way: exporting without registering

A related but distinct gap: writing a value to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT exports it to later steps, but does not, by itself, tell the runner to mask it anywhere.

- env:
    API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
  run: echo "token=$API_TOKEN" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

Here the value written is the original secret string, so GitHub's masking actually does still catch it if a later step echoes $API_TOKEN directly by that same route. The sharper version of this gap is a freshly derived value — an OAuth token your workflow mints using the secret, a signed URL, a short-lived session cookie. That value was never declared as a secret to the runner at all, so it is not on the masking list regardless of how it is printed, until the workflow explicitly calls:

echo "::add-mask::$DERIVED_TOKEN"

The fix

  • Avoid transforming a secret in any step whose output is logged. If you need a fingerprint or a check value, compute it from something that is not secret, or accept that the transformed value needs its own mask.
  • If a step must print or export a transformed or derived value, call ::add-mask:: on that exact value before the line that could print it.
  • Treat anything written to $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT/$GITHUB_STATE that originated from a secret as needing its own explicit mask — do not assume export implies masked.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Secret Leak Check to find every transformed-secret and unmasked-env-export finding across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow has either pattern — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean your secrets are safe — only that these two documented patterns were not found.
